🏭 Lean Six Sigma 

One common mistake in organizations is trying to use Lean Six Sigma for every problem.

💡 Lean Six Sigma is most effective when the both problem and solution is unknown.

If the solution is already obvious, standard problem-solving tools, SOPs, or corrective actions can often resolve the issue faster.

Use Lean Six Sigma when:
✅ Root cause is unclear
✅ Multiple factors affect the outcome
✅ Data analysis is required
✅ Previous fixes have failed
✅ Breakthrough improvement is needed

🎯 The goal is not to use the most advanced tool, but the right tool for the right problem.

Right Problem + Right Tool = Right Result

🏭 Lean Manufacturing Excellence starts with measuring work accurately.

In manufacturing, productivity is not improved by working faster—it is improved by establishing the right standards and continuously improving them.

One of the most important Industrial Engineering metrics is SMV (Standard Minute Value).

📊 What is SMV?

SMV is the standard time required for a qualified operator to complete one unit of work using the defined method under normal working conditions.

🔹 Components of SMV

✅ Observed Time (OT)
✅ Performance Rating (PR)
✅ Normal Time (NT)
✅ Allowances (Personal, Fatigue & Delay)
✅ Standard Time (ST)

🔹 Typical Allowances

👤 Personal Allowance: 5–7%
💪 Fatigue Allowance: 8–12%
⏳ Delay Allowance: 3–8%

Typical Total Allowance = 15–25%

🔹 SMV Formula
SMV = Normal Time × (1 + Allowance %)

Where:

Normal Time = Observed Time × Performance Rating

🔹 Why is SMV Important?

✔ Production Planning & Scheduling
✔ Capacity Planning
✔ Manpower Planning
✔ Line Balancing
✔ Cost Estimation
✔ Productivity Measurement
✔ Incentive Calculations

💡 Example

Observed Time = 70 sec
Performance Rating = 110%
Allowance = 20%

➡ Normal Time = 1.284 min

➡ SMV = 1.541 min/unit

This means a trained operator following the standard method should take 1.541 minutes to produce one unit.

🎯 Key Insight

Without an accurate SMV:

❌ Capacity calculations become unreliable
❌ Production targets become unrealistic
❌ Manpower planning becomes inaccurate
❌ Productivity measurement loses meaning

Accurate SMV is the foundation of Lean Manufacturing Excellence, enabling organizations to balance resources, improve efficiency, and make data-driven decisions.

🚀 You cannot improve productivity unless you first establish the standard.

🏭 Lean Manufacturing Excellence starts with understanding work at the motion level.

Many organizations focus on improving output, but sustainable productivity improvement begins with understanding how work is actually performed.

This is where MTM (Methods-Time Measurement) and MOST (Maynard Operation Sequence Technique) become powerful Industrial Engineering tools.

📊 Both are Predetermined Motion Time Systems (PMTS) used to establish standard times without relying solely on stopwatch studies.

🔹 MTM – Methods-Time Measurement

MTM analyzes basic human motions such as:
✅ Reach
✅ Grasp
✅ Move
✅ Position
✅ Release

It provides highly accurate standard times and is ideal for detailed method improvement and workstation design.

🔹 MOST – Maynard Operation Sequence Technique

MOST focuses on motion sequences rather than individual motions.

Benefits include:
✅ Faster analysis
✅ Easier implementation
✅ Suitable for high-volume manufacturing environments
✅ Effective for process planning and capacity estimation

🎯 MTM vs MOST

🔹 MTM = Higher Accuracy + Detailed Analysis
🔹 MOST = Faster Application + Practical Implementation

Both methods help organizations:

✔ Establish standard work
✔ Improve line balancing
✔ Reduce cycle time
✔ Optimize manpower utilization
✔ Improve productivity
✔ Support Lean Manufacturing Excellence

💡 You cannot improve what you cannot measure.

Understanding motion, eliminating waste, and standardizing work are the foundations of world-class manufacturing.

🚀 Manufacturing Excellence is achieved when every motion adds value and every process is continuously improved.

items.content:
🏭 Performance Rating – The Heart of Accurate Time Study

In Industrial Engineering,
measuring time alone is not enough.

Two operators may complete the same task in different times due to differences in skill, effort, experience, and working methods. This is where Performance Rating (PR)becomes critical.

📊 What is Performance Rating?

Performance Rating is the assessment of an operator's working pace compared to a qualified worker performing at a normal speed.

Its purpose is to convert Observed Time (OT) into Normal Time (NT)and establish fair, realistic, and achievable standards.

🔹 Why Performance Rating is Important?

✅ Eliminates bias from fast or slow operators
✅ Establishes realistic standard times
✅ Improves capacity planning accuracy
✅ Supports manpower planning
✅ Enables accurate SMV calculation
✅ Improves productivity measurement
✅ Strengthens Lean Manufacturing Excellence

🔹 Typical Rating Scale

🔹 80% – Slow
🔹 90% – Below Normal
🔹 100% – Normal
🔹 110% – Good
🔹 120% – Fast
🔹 130% – Very Fast

🔹 Factors Considered During Rating

✔ Skill
✔ Effort
✔ Working Conditions
✔ Consistency

🔹 Components of SMV

1️⃣ Observed Time (OT)
2️⃣ Performance Rating (PR)
3️⃣ Normal Time (NT)
4️⃣ Allowances
5️⃣ Standard Time (ST)
6️⃣ SMV (Standard Minute Value)

🔹 Typical Allowances

👤 Personal Allowance = 5–7%
💪 Fatigue Allowance = 8–12%
⏳ Delay Allowance = 3–8%

Total Typical Allowance = 15–25%

🔹 SMV Formula

Normal Time (NT) = OT × PR / 100

Standard Time (ST) = NT × (1 + Allowance %)

SMV = Standard Time

🔹 Example

Observed Time = 70 sec

Performance Rating = 110%

Allowance = 20%

➡ Normal Time = 77 sec

➡ Standard Time = 92.4 sec

➡ SMV = 1.54 min/unit

🎯 Key Insight

Without proper Performance Rating:

❌ Standard Times become inaccurate
❌ Capacity calculations become unreliable
❌ Production targets become unrealistic
❌ Productivity measurements lose credibility

A stopwatch records time, but Performance Rating converts that time into a meaningful standard.

🚀 Accurate standards lead to accurate planning, and accurate planning drives Manufacturing Excellence.

🏭 Lean Manufacturing Excellence starts with understanding every motion.

Many organizations focus on machines, automation, and technology to improve productivity. However, one of the biggest opportunities for improvement lies in the way people perform their work.

This is where PMTS (Predetermined Motion Time System)plays a vital role.

PMTS is an Industrial Engineering technique that breaks a task into basic human motions such as Reach, Grasp, Move, Position, and Release, assigning a standard time value to each motion based on scientific data.

📊 Why PMTS matters?

✅ Establishes accurate standard times
✅ Eliminates unnecessary motions and waste
✅ Improves productivity and line balancing
✅ Supports capacity and manpower planning
✅ Reduces dependency on subjective performance ratings
✅ Strengthens Lean Manufacturing Excellence

Example:

Task: Pick and Place a Component

🔹 Reach = 8 TMU
🔹 Grasp = 3 TMU
🔹 Move = 12 TMU
🔹 Position = 6 TMU
🔹 Release = 1 TMU

Total = 30 TMU

Since 1 TMU = 0.036 seconds,

⏱ Standard Time = 30 × 0.036 = **1.08 seconds**

The real value of PMTS is not just in calculating time—it is in designing better methods, eliminating waste, and creating sustainable productivity improvements.

💡 Every unnecessary motion is a hidden cost. Eliminating it today improves performance tomorrow.

✅ SUM() – Calculate total production, output, or defects.

✅ AVERAGE() – Find average SMV, efficiency, or cycle time.

✅ IF() – Automate decisions based on production conditions.

✅ COUNTIF() – Count defects, delays, or operators meeting targets.

✅ SUMIF() – Sum production or defects based on specific criteria.

✅ VLOOKUP() / XLOOKUP() – Retrieve SMVs, operator details, or style information instantly.

✅ INDEX() + MATCH() – A more flexible alternative to VLOOKUP for accurate data retrieval.

✅ ROUND() – Standardize efficiency percentages and production calculations.

✅ TEXT() – Format reports, dates, and production summaries professionally.

✅ Pivot Tables – Transform thousands of production records into meaningful insights within seconds.

The Planner Roles: Who Does What in Supply Chain Planning?

In a well-structured supply chain, planners have distinct but complementary responsibilities that ensure alignment from demand forecasting to material availability.

Overview of the 4 key roles:

1. Demand Planner – Predicts future demand based on historical sales, market trends, and stakeholder inputs.
2. Supply Planner – Aligns demand, capacity, and inventory. Defines inventory targets to hit service levels.
3. Production Planner – Schedules production balances batches and constraints using ERP and capacity data.
4. Material Planner – Ensures raw materials are available when needed and monitors live stock data.

Each role contributes to ensuring product availability, optimizing stock levels, and supporting efficient operations.

Different MRP Procedures Used In SAP PP Explained with a Motorcycle Manufacturing Example 🏍️
In manufacturing, one important thing to understand is:
Not every material should be planned the same way.
Imagine a motorcycle manufacturing company 🏭
For every motorcycle, the company needs engines, frames, tyres, batteries, brake assemblies, nuts, bolts, lubricants, and packaging materials.
Now the question is:
Should all these materials follow the same planning method?
The answer is no.
That is where MRP procedures come in.
An MRP procedure decides when and how much material should be procured or produced.
There are two main approaches:
1. MRP Planning 📊
MRP is used when demand depends on the production plan, sales orders, forecast, or BOM.
Example:
If the company plans to produce 1,000 motorcycles, the system calculates:
1,000 engines
2,000 tyres
1,000 batteries
1,000 brake assemblies
This happens through the Bill of Materials.
MRP is best for critical and high-value production materials like engines, frames, tyres, batteries, and brake assemblies.
2. Consumption-Based Planning 📦
Consumption-based planning works differently.
Here, the system looks at stock levels, past consumption, or fixed planning intervals instead of mainly depending on the production plan.
Example:
Nuts, bolts, washers, lubricants, gloves, and packaging materials are used regularly in a motorcycle plant.
Instead of planning them for every motorcycle order, the system can say:
“When stock goes below a certain level, reorder again.”
This is useful for low-value and frequently used materials.
Types of Consumption-Based Planning 🔁
Reorder Point Planning:
When stock falls below a set level, the system suggests replenishment.
Manual Reorder Point: The planner sets the reorder level manually.
Automatic Reorder Point: The system calculates it using past consumption, lead time, and safety stock.
Forecast-Based Planning 📈: The system predicts future demand from past consumption.
Time-Phased Planning 🗓️: Planning happens on fixed days, such as every Monday.
Simple Difference
MRP is based on future requirements.
Consumption-based planning is based on past usage or stock levels.
So, in a motorcycle company:
Use MRP for engines, frames, tyres, batteries, and brake assemblies.
Use consumption-based planning for nuts, bolts, washers, lubricants, gloves, and packaging materials.
A good production planner avoids: Material shortages that stop production
Excess inventory that blocks working capital
Planning is not just about creating orders.
It is about choosing the right planning method for the right material. ✅

𝗟𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗘𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 % 𝘃𝘀 𝗔𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝗘𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆

One number for management. One number for you.

𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗺𝘂𝗹𝗮:
 `Line Efficiency % = [Σ SMV × Actual Output pcs] / [Total Operators × Working Minutes] × 100`

𝗗𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗘𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲:

Style SMV = 12.55 min/pc  
Output = 50 dozen = 600 pcs  
Operators = 26, Working time = 435 min  
`Numerator = 12.55 × 600 = 7530 min`  
`Denominator = 26 × 435 = 11310 min`  
`Efficiency = 7530 / 11310 × 100 = 66.55%`

*Wait, why not 80%?* Because 80% is “Achieved Efficiency” = `Actual Output / Target Output`  
`Target = [22 × 435] / 12.55 = 901 pcs`  
`Achieved = 7350 / 11310 = 66.55%` Same thing.

𝗜𝗘 𝗗𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘆 𝗨𝘀𝗲: 

1. Calculate at 10 AM and 2 PM. Don’t wait till evening.

2. If <40% by lunch, you’ve lost the day. Pull floater, break balance, cut WIP now.

3. Show this number to supervisor, not “line looks busy”.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁: 

You can show 80% by making low SMV style. Profit is still low. Use SMV-based efficiency only.

Do you calculate both or just one?

👉 Resources

👉 Labour utilization

✔ Analyze load vs available hours
✔ Balance manpower and machine utilization
✔ Reduce overload and idle capacity

🚧 Bottleneck Analysis

✔ Identify process constraints early
✔ Monitor bottleneck resources continuously
✔ Improve throughput and production flow

⚖️ Load vs Capacity

✔ Compare planned load against actual capacity
✔ Perform RCCP before execution
✔ Support subcontracting or alternate planning when required

💡 **Key Insight:**
Strong Capacity Planning helps organizations:
✅ Reduce firefighting
✅ Improve on-time delivery
✅ Increase utilization
✅ Prevent production delays
✅ Improve planning stability

🚀 Effective S&OP succeeds when:
Demand + Capacity + Material + Resources
are aligned in one realistic execution plan.

items.content:
"The foundation of quality is the human being. No drawing, no process, no document will save it." the MD of ELGI EQUIPMENTS LIMITED said this to me on our podcast when I asked how ELGi protects quality at the production level.

ELGi has zero contract labour on their production floor. Workers go through three years of vocational training before they are considered fully capable. 

Shop floor attrition is effectively zero. The only contractors on site handle housekeeping, the canteen, and material movement.

The MD was specific about why.

"The person's feel when a nut does not rotate smoothly is an indicator. If that person's mind and heart are not committed, no process and no document is going to protect it."

That feel is not trained in a week. It is built over years of repetition, ownership, and the belief that the work matters. You cannot contract for it.

I think about this when I visit plants across India and watch the trend continue in the other direction. Contract labour at sixty percent. Seventy. In some companies, ninety percent of the production workforce. The rationale is flexibility and cost. Both are real.

What is not written on any balance sheet is the ceiling this places on quality.

Building a world-class product is not unlike building a world-class athlete. Sania Mirza did not become what she became through a series of annual contracts. The capability is accumulated. It cannot be borrowed on demand.

The Japanese companies I studied in the 1980s treated production workers as the carriers of institutional knowledge, not as replaceable units of labour. 

Toyota's improvement systems were not designed by engineers and handed down. They were built with the people doing the work, because those people knew something no specification sheet could capture.

If you cannot earn the mind and heart of a person who is here for one year, you have already decided what quality ceiling you can live with.

Most companies have simply not written that decision down.

Demand Variability vs Forecast Error: What Planners Must Understand!
Unstable demand and poor forecasting are not the same problem.
But many planning teams treat them as if they are.
When demand goes up and down, the first reaction is often:
“The forecast is wrong.”
But sometimes, the forecast is not the real issue.
Sometimes, the demand pattern itself is naturally unstable.
What is Demand Variability?
Demand variability means actual customer demand keeps changing.
It is usually caused by:
📈 Seasonality — demand rises and falls during specific periods
 📢 Promotions — campaigns create temporary spikes
 👥 Customer behavior — order frequency or quantity changes
 🌍 Market changes — competition, pricing, or demand shifts
 🏗️ Project-based demand — irregular bulk orders
 🚀 Product lifecycle changes — launch, growth, maturity, or decline
What is Forecast Error?
Forecast error means the forecast is different from actual demand.
It answers:
🎯 “How wrong was the forecast?”
Demand variability answers:
📊 “How unstable is the demand pattern?”
Why the Difference Matters
A stable product with high forecast error needs better planning discipline.
That may mean:
🧹 Cleaner data
 🧠 Better assumptions
 🤝 Improved sales input
 📅 Stronger S&OP alignment
 🔍 Review of forecast bias
 ⚙️ Better planning parameters
But a highly variable product may need a different planning strategy.
That may mean:
📦 SKU segmentation
 🛡️ Safety stock strategy
 👁️ Customer visibility
 ⏱️ Lead time review
 🚨 Exception-based planning
 📊 Different service-level rules

Great planners do not only ask:
“Was the forecast accurate?”
They also ask:
“Was this demand pattern forecastable?”
🎯 Forecast error tells you how wrong the forecast was.
📊 Demand variability tells you how unstable the demand pattern is.
Both matter.
Which creates more issues in your planning process — demand variability or forecast error?

🏭 Line Layout Types: U-Shape vs Straight vs Modular
Which layout delivers the best production efficiency?

There isn't a single "best" layout—the right choice depends on your product, order size, and production strategy.

🔹 1. Straight Line Layout

✅ Best for high-volume, repetitive production
✔ Easy to manage and monitor
✔ Simple material flow
❌ Longer walking distance for supervisors and helpers
❌ Less flexible for style changes

🔹 2. U-Shape Layout

✅ Best for Lean Manufacturing
✔ Shorter material movement
✔ Better communication between operators
✔ Faster problem-solving
✔ Reduced WIP and improved line balancing
📈 Often delivers higher efficiency in balanced production lines.

🔹 3. Modular Layout

✅ Best for small batches and frequent style changes
✔ Multi-skilled operators
✔ High flexibility
✔ Faster response to customer demand
❌ Requires skilled teamwork and cross-training.

📊 Example (Denim Pants Production)

A factory producing 1,200 denim pants/day compared three layouts:

🔸 Straight Line → 72% Efficiency
🔸 U-Shape → 82% Efficiency
🔸 Modular → 87% Efficiency (after operator training)

Key Lesson:
The highest efficiency doesn't come from the layout alone—it comes from proper line balancing, standard work, operator skills, and continuous improvement.

💬 Which layout does your factory use, and what efficiency do you achieve? Share your experience in the comments!

🏭 Master the Manufacturing Flow: Is Your Bottleneck Running You?
 
In manufacturing, a system is only as strong as its weakest link. If you aren't actively managing your constraint, that constraint is managing your entire plant's output.
 
To transition from local "efficiencies" to global system excellence, the Theory of Constraints (TOC) provides a proven roadmap for the shop floor:
 
🚀 The Five Focusing Steps for Continuous Improvement:
 
Identify the system constraint.
Exploit the constraint (ensure not a single minute of bottleneck time is wasted).
Subordinate everything else (align all non-constraints to support the bottleneck's pace).
Elevate the constraint (invest in more capacity only after steps 1-3 are exhausted).
Repeat (don't let inertia become the next constraint).
 
📊 The Three Key Measures of Success: Traditional cost accounting can be misleading. TOC simplifies your focus into three manufacturing-specific metrics:
 
Throughput (T): The rate at which the system generates money through sales (Revenue minus raw material costs).
Inventory (I): All the money tied up in raw materials, work-in-process (WIP), and finished goods.
Operating Expense (OE): All the money spent turning inventory into throughput (labour, utilities, etc.).
 
⚙️ Execution & Scheduling:
 
Drum-Buffer-Rope (DBR): The "Production Engine" that synchronizes the plant's pace to the constraint, using time buffers to protect the flow and a "rope" to pull work only when the system can handle it.
Throughput per Constraint Minute (T/CM): The "Scheduling Brain" that prioritises jobs based on how much global profit they generate per minute of bottleneck time, rather than just per-unit margins.
 
Stop chasing 100% efficiency on every machine and start focusing on the flow that matters. 🚀

🏭 Manufacturing Is More Than Just Machining!

Many people associate manufacturing only with CNC Turning, Milling, and Drilling. However, a complete manufacturing ecosystem consists of dozens of interconnected processes that transform raw materials into finished products.

A comprehensive manufacturing process chain includes:

✅ Casting Processes
✅ Forging & Forming Processes
✅ Sheet Metal Operations
✅ CNC Machining Processes
✅ Laser Cutting & Water Jet Cutting
✅ Welding & Joining Technologies
✅ Heat Treatment Processes
✅ Surface Finishing & Coating
✅ Additive Manufacturing (3D Printing)
✅ Non-Conventional Machining (EDM, Wire EDM, ECM, etc.)
✅ Molding Processes
✅ Inspection & Quality Control Systems

Every process has a direct impact on: 🔹 Product Quality
🔹 Manufacturing Cost
🔹 Lead Time
🔹 Tool Life
🔹 Production Efficiency
🔹 Customer Satisfaction

The most successful manufacturing organizations don't focus on a single process—they optimize the entire value chain from raw material procurement to final inspection and dispatch.

Understanding how these processes interact helps engineers, production planners, quality teams, and management make better decisions, reduce hidden costs, and improve overall operational performance.

📊 Manufacturing excellence is achieved when every process is understood, controlled, and continuously improved.

"The Monday morning crisis call didn't happen."
That's what a supply chain director told me six months after they went live with DDMRP.

It didn't happen. 
They cancelled it. 
There was nothing to crisis-manage.

I've sat in dozens of those Monday morning exception meetings. The screen full of red. The procurement team defending last week's decisions. The ops director asking why they're out of a part that's been on the shortage list for three weeks. Everyone busy, nothing resolved, Tuesday already looking the same.

The meeting is a feature of how the priority system works.

MRP generates more exceptions than any team can meaningfully act on. So the Monday meeting becomes triage theater, an expensive and exhausting ritual that creates the feeling of control without the reality of it. That ritual costs, conservatively:
→ 8 people, 90 minutes, weekly = 12 hours of senior time per week
→ 624 hours per year on one meeting
→ Decisions made under time pressure with incomplete information

When planners have 12 real signals instead of 400 noise events, the war room becomes unnecessary. They know on Friday what needs attention on Monday.

"We still meet," the director told me. "But now we talk about strategy. About what we're going to improve. Not what we're going to survive."

What does your Monday morning meeting actually solve?

Planning debt.
That's what I call it.

It compounds like financial debt, but you pay the interest in emergency freight, planner attrition, and customer failures that could have been caught six weeks earlier.

I spoke to a planning team last week paying north of R20M a year in expedite fees alone. Two planners had left in 18 months. When I asked their lead planner what a normal Tuesday looked like, she had to think about it.

"Honestly? I don't know what normal is anymore. Every Tuesday is different. But every Tuesday is the same kind of different. Something's on fire, and by end of day we're already worried about Wednesday."

Nine years in supply chain. Brilliant at the job. The system won't let her do it.

MRP generates exceptions faster than any team can clear them, so they triage instead of plan. The debt accumulates quietly. "I'll get to proper planning next week" stops being said out loud, because everyone knows it won't happen next week either.

Change the priority system and the triage stops. 12 real signals instead of 400 noise events. Planning becomes possible again.

How deep is the planning debt in your organisation?

Moody's titled a 2025 report: "Tariffs don't break supply chains; financial fragility does."

They're right. And it runs deeper than they say.

When the tariffs hit, most companies did the same thing. They bought ahead. Pull the inventory forward, beat the cost increase, protect the line.

Days of inventory on hand jumped 228% between February and April 2025, as firms raced to stock up ahead of the tariffs.

Here's what that actually was.

Not resilience. A working capital transfer. You convert cash into inventory at a higher landed cost, freeze it on the balance sheet, and take on the obsolescence risk yourself.

And the bill comes later.

The WTO reported that this frontloading lifted world trade in 2025, then cut its 2026 goods trade growth forecast to 0.5%. The demand was pulled forward, not created. What follows a pull-forward is a purge.

→ Tariff announced
→ Panic buy inflates the order signal
→ Real demand comes in lower
→ Inventory glut, then a destock

We watched semiconductors do exactly this. Famine to glut in eighteen months. Now the whole economy is running the same play against a tariff clock.

The tariff was a one-time cost line. The panic response is a recurring wound on the balance sheet.

A tariff doesn't break a chain that can absorb variability. It breaks one that can only react.

Demand-driven buffers, positioned at the right points, absorb the shock instead of amplifying it. You decouple from the disruption rather than passing it down the line at 228%.

Stop stockpiling against fear. Start positioning for flow.

items.content:
Toyota started 2026 with 33 days of new-vehicle supply.

Volkswagen started 2026 with 143.

Same country. Same year. Same tariffs.

That 110-day gap is not a demand story. It's a planning story.

Two groups of OEMs faced the same conditions. One ran lean buffers tied to actual consumption. The other planned multi-year capital deployment against an EV adoption forecast that did not materialize.

The results are in the filings:

→ EV days-of-supply hit 168 days in January 2026. ICE sat at 97. The widest gap on record (Cox Automotive).
→ Ford booked $19.5 billion in charges in December 2025, including an $8.5 billion Model E write-down.
→ Stellantis reported negative €6 billion in FY2024 industrial free cash flow, citing "temporarily elevated working capital."

That's CFO language for "the inventory plan was wrong."

The supplier base is paying the bill the OEMs forecast:

→ Marelli filed Chapter 11 in June 2025 with $4.9 billion in funded debt.
→ First Brands (FRAM, Raybestos) filed in September 2025 with $6 billion in debt and $4 billion off-balance-sheet.

They didn't fail because tariffs hit 25%. They failed because OEM demand collapsed against the forecast they had built capacity to serve.

AlixPartners 2025 revised the US EV forecast down 46%. When you plan multi-year capital deployment against a forecast, the forecast becomes a single point of failure for your balance sheet.

Toyota didn't dodge the EV trap by predicting better.

Toyota dodged it by carrying less forecast risk.
